chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

It is not befitting for the man who is not in Ihram to marry the one in Ihram, while he knows that it is not permissible for him. I said to him, 'What if he does so and the one in Ihram has intercourse with her?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'If they were both knowing, then upon each one of them is a sacrificial animal (Badanah). And upon the woman, if she was in Ihram, is a sacrificial animal, and if she was not in Ihram, there is nothing upon her, except if she had known that the one who married her was in Ihram. So if she knew, then married him, then upon her is a sacrificial animal.'

key_terms.الْحَلَال: The one who is not in Ihram (permissible state)
key_terms.بَدَنَة: A specific type of sacrificial animal (usually a camel or cow) used as a penalty
key_terms.مُحْرِمٌ: One in the state of Ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)

ai.seo_question: What is the penalty for a non-Ihram man marrying a woman in Ihram?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the financial penalty (Badanah) for a non-Ihram man marrying an Ihram woman, emphasizing that liability is contingent upon mutual knowledge of the prohibition. It distinguishes the woman's liability based on her own state of Ihram and her awareness of her husband's status, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that ignorance can exempt one from specific sacrificial dues. This ruling underscores the importance of conscious adherence to Hajj restrictions within marital contracts during the sacred state.
